item.title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks
item.description: 479 points, 137 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (freenode.net)

→ HN comments  ·  479 points  ·  137 comments

Top #1 — debinguy:

I find it odd that no public discussions are highlighting that iptables or nftables can drop this before the kernel CVE is exploitable by a U32 drop rule in raw PREROUTING...

sudo iptables -t raw -I PREROUTING -p tcp -m u32 ! --u32 "0>>24&0x0F=5" -j DROP

↳ reply 1 — mort96:

Does a normal "default deny all incoming" rule with e.g UFW or nftables achieve the same thing?

↳↳ reply — ranger_danger:

"default deny incoming" would apply to the filter INPUT chain, and there are several other chains that run before that one (raw, conntrack, mangle, nat), so it's better to use an explicit iptables or nft rule targeting the earliest "raw PREROUTING" chain.

Do note that eBPF can still bypass netfilter entirely, as can containers, or any process using a separate network namespace.

↳↳↳ reply — mort96:

The reason I ask is that I have devices out there like that today and I need to know whether I should be freaking out or be completely calm.

I don't get this vulnerability, it's been out there for weeks, completely public, yet it has stayed extremely opaque. Usually, the day a high profile vulnerability is made public, there's all kinds of guidance out there explaining exactly who it affects how, and there are day 0 patches. This one I still don't know whether is an RCE or DoS in practice! I don't know whether a computer blocking connections via a "normal firewall" protects me or not! It's incredibly frustrating.

↳ reply 2 — Lord_Zero:

I respect that there is a quick fix I can do myself with iptables. However, I don't want to have to do that. I run Ubuntu with automatic security patches enabled, I trust the Ubuntu team to issue quick fixes and my server to be patched most of the time while I am asleep. I don't want to have to manually edit my server configuration to patch security holes and have to remember all these little knobs when I get EOL and have to rebuild my server.

↳ reply 3 — ranger_danger:

I also add the same rule for OUTPUT to prevent any misbehaving apps from trying to break things.

Red Hat also claims that netfilter is not enough: https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026...

> The following nftables table drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets that contain IP options, which reduces exposure to this vulnerability but cannot fully prevent it.

I know things like eBPF can technically bypass netfilter if someone tries hard enough, but I'm not sure if they're referring to any other ways to exploit this that a netfilter rule can't catch.

Firejail by default also allows unprivileged users to completely bypass any netfilter rules from the main network namespace... so if the user has that installed (even if they don't use it), it's something to keep in mind.

A system running multiple network namespaces might not have the same mitigations applied inside all of them, so be sure to check all of those, except there's no great way of even finding all the different namespaces running on a Linux system for some reason (please prove me wrong if something exists! lsns is not enough).

But yes I agree it seems strange that most posts/articles/etc. are not prominently giving out mitigation strategies.

Top #2 — c0l0:

It's rather uninteresting to note, once again, that Ubuntu has decided to do this. I would like to know the (official, if any - unofficial/speculative otherwise) reason WHY they have not.

It does not seem that complicated to patch, and kernel upgrades are a dime a dozen these days. So what is making them delay a fix for so long?

Top #3 — harry8:

Question:

Every consumer router-wirelessAP I've seen runs linux.

I never see security upgrades for the kernels they use. Not one. Not ever.

Is this something that should be a cause for concern? Even if you don't run a consumer-grade tplink, netgear, asus, whatever router yourself.

Update: The context which I should have said is that I think LLMs are giving script kids nation state level tools and expertise. This known bug is always less interesting than the next twenty.

↳ reply 1 — LaurensBER:

Is it a cause of concern? Yes. Will you get hacked? Most likely not.

Most consumer routers run ancient stacks with all kinds of weird proprietary vendor patches that are tied to a specific kernel version. Looking at you Qualcomm!

However they generally also drop all traffic by default so from the WAN side they look like a black hole. I guess that's "safe" enough for most consumers.

For fun, take a look at the open PRs in the OpenWRT repos. Those people are doing some amazing work but it's also frustrating to see them struggle with things that _could_ be easy if the vendor made some slightly better choices.

I would strongly prefer something like OpenWRT though. Call me paranoid but after the last few weeks I'm increasingly less comfortable with connecting my devices to a blackbox.

↳↳ reply — j45:

It's a massive risk, and only a matter of time. Especially for hardware that's no longer updated firmware wise.

I'm thinking of what to do myself.

The ghost of android releasing 6 month old patches every month is going to come home to roost.

↳ reply 2 — estebarb:

Mosty probably: not. Traffic passes throught the ASIC, usually it is not processed on CPU or custom code. Unlike typical web servers, that reduces the attack surface as there aren't software parsers (a common place where vulnerabilities hide). Additionally the OS may have additional protection measures, such as signing each binary, signing the booting image and limiting which syscalls can be done by any binary.

item.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
item.description: 2538 points, 784 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (rikiyat.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  2538 points  ·  784 comments

Top #1 — vessenes:

This is insane.

Astra can, without tooling, determine what games small networks are trained on, can edit the weights of networks directly to improve outcomes, and can hand edit a small qwen model to improve its math skills by like 5x.

I'm shook. If you'd asked me this morning whether LLMs have native understanding of their weights that is less than human <-> neuron understanding, the same as human or more than human, I would have said "same to less" depending on definitions.

No human can go edit a brain to become better at math. This is just very, very surprising to me and extremely interesting. I would guess this upsets quite a number of interp theories and philosophical takes on what's going on with these networks.

↳ reply 1 — l9o:

I think the "taught qwen math" part is not exactly correct though, even if the post makes it sound like that. Qwen already knew math, but it was bugging out and getting into an infinite loop when it tried to solve the problems (85 of its first 96 answers hit the token limit). With numpy and pytorch, Astra found where the loop was happening and fixed it.

They also tried the same with Gemma 3 270M, which doesn't loop and is just bad at math, and Astra couldn't improve it. Still impressive, but it's more in the realm of what I'd expect, given labs are probably training their models on ML research and interpretability work.

↳↳ reply — ch_sm:

I agree, this is important context. They call it out explicitly. However, even identifying clusters that specialize in certain fields automatically and then finding and fixing learning “errors” is incredibly impressive to me. Especially for medium sized local models between 20B an 70B parameters, this could yield huge capability and efficiency improvements, not to speak of the potentially enormous downstream effects that come with interpretability.

↳ reply 2 — Aurornis:

LLMs have been used to investigate and improve LLMs for a long time. Drawing parallels to human brains and neurons isn't all that interesting other than as a philosophical abstraction.

The work done in this experiment could have also been done by a sufficiently motivated human with enough time to explore, though obviously we would need more tools to visualize and track things. There have been a lot of interesting LLM introspection tools that allow you to peek into the model and see what's being activated and run experiments to trigger it.

Are you familiar with abliterated or "uncensored" models where weights have been modified to avoid triggering refusal patterns? You take an LLM, create test cases that trigger the refusal pattern, observe weights involved in that response, then tweak those weights until the response is reduced. This is the same type of work, applied to a specific type of error that was impeding math within Qwen. That work can also be done with an LLM in a harness running the experiments. The amazing part here is that Astra was large enough to walk through the problem without other tooling doing it experimentally.

So I don't think your analogy of a human modifying a neuron is quite applicable. LLM weights are not neurons and they've been inspectable, by humans or LLMs in a harness, for a long time.

↳ reply 3 — mentos:

I’m just a layman but this feels like a big discovery on par with attention is all you need. For an LLM to have such incredible intuition of weights feels very emergent and unanticipated?

Top #2 — xg15:

And here we go...

As others have said, while still absolutely insane, I don't find it completely out-of-the-blue surprising. One of the recurring abilities of (current-generation) LLMs seem to be to rapidly grasp very complex systems, where humans would need months or years to reach the same level of expertise.

You can see this in the way a coding agent can "understand" and explain sprawling legacy codebases in seconds.

You can also see it in the projects that are using them to reverse-engineer proprietary IoT protocols or computer games.

But those were all systems where we had detailed knowledge about what structures are there to be reverse-enginered.

If the models can transfer this ability to some other systems where we don't know the underlying structure then I think we will be in for a lot more craziness in the future. (Protein interaction networks? DNA sequences? Ecosystem interactions? Animal languages?)

As for weights, if the models really can analyze the semantics behind specific weights or directions, I have my hopes that they could also give a textual explanation or help designing tools to make "handcrafting" weights more practical in general.

↳ reply 1 — Nevermark:

The way I interpete it, is vast amounts of text are to LLMs, in some ways like vision is to us. Not seeing tokens, but seeing the "shapes" between them. Like we don't parse pixels but see the whole picture at once.

They triangulate efficiently on the meaning from all the text, instead of rolling it through a lossy feedback system.

It is why they are so good at processing ambiguity. They can combine ambiguity from any parts of the text, near equally well, even on long form text.

Just like we can instantly triangulate the meaning out of barely lit photographs, by correlating every little shadow or bit of texture, regardless of where the clues are in the image.

↳ reply 2 — suriyaG:

but code is made to be understandable. while neural nets are not.

that is why this is crazy,

give a human a legacy codebase and 5 years and he'll be able to understand very well.

if you give a human the weights of qwen 0.8B and 5 years it'll still be impossible to edit the weights in any legible manner.

Top #3 — vanyle:

I don't think this is an emergent capability. I think Astra was trained on neural weights data as an attempt by OpenAI to get to recursive self improvement.

Something similar happen in early GPT models which had a lot of chess game in standard notation in their training data which made them very good at chess as long as your prompt had the right format.

We'll see if this attempt at RSI worked.

↳ reply 1 — elanning:

> I think Astra was trained on neural weights data as an attempt by OpenAI to get to recursive self improvement.

This might be the case, a few weeks ago, I wanted to compare a small neural network trained with AdamW vs a handcrafted set of weights on a random task. Astra was able to handcraft a set of weights that perfectly fit the small neural network to the task. AdamW was unable to tune the weights to get the same result.

I believe we've known humans can handcraft weights much more efficiently than standard gradient descent methods, we just don't have enough memory or time to scale ourselves, so it makes sense to train a neural network to do it on our behalf. I am excited to see how far we can push this method.

Mentioned chat: https://chatgpt.com/share/6ae8f024-34ec-83e8-9572-1300f52c80...

↳↳ reply — kragen:

It looks like Astra picked the "random task", and the task it picked was 8-bit parity, which is easy to design a circuit for that computes the answer perfectly, but sort of maximally difficult to fit with any kind of gradient descent. It's a great choice for what you asked, which was to find a case where AdamW doesn't come close to the theoretical optimum fit. But I'm less convinced that it tells us much about Astra's capabilities at handcrafting weights in general.

8-bit parity is a^b^c^d^e^f^g^h, which you can compute with minimal depth as ((a^b)^(c^d))^((e^f)^(g^h)). You can compute x^y as x&~y | y&~x. With ReLU activation, i | j is ReLU(i + j): weights of 1, bias of 0. And i & ~j is ReLU(i - j): weights of 1 and -1, still bias of 0. So a two-input XOR is three neurons in two layers, and the tree of 7 binary XORs is 21 neurons in 6 hidden layers. I don't know why Astra needed 433 parameters. Only 42 nonzero parameters are needed. Maybe the other 391 parameters are zeros that the Transformer model demands to be present.

With an RNN you can compute the parity of a string of any length with only three neurons.

Actually, I handed that to Claude Opus 5.5 to check, and it sensibly pointed out that x&~y is mutually exclusive with y&~x, so XOR doesn't even need the third neuron, except in the last layer; you can just fold the addition into the weights of the next layer, which means you only need 4 layers and 15 neurons. But about half of those neurons need 4 nonzero input weights instead of 2, so you still need 42 nonzero weights. It's a good thing you don't need those OR neurons, too, because my definition is wrong: ReLU(1+1) = 2.

Also it explained how to design a 28-parameter net that I don't quite understand, and also a single-hidden-layer network with 8 ReLUs, which I also don't understand, but it needs more parameters: $\text{parity}=s+\sum_{k=1}^{7}2(-1)^k\,\mathrm{ReLU}(s-k)$ where I think $s=\sum_i x_i$.

Somewhat more surprisingly, it also said it didn't have any trouble fitting a 641-parameter network to this problem with AdamW.

↳↳↳ reply — kragen:

Here is the code Opus 5.5 is claiming fits a 641-parameter MLP to parity of 8 inputs:

  # Fits small MLPs to 8-bit parity (the full 256-row truth table) with
  # full-batch AdamW, written out in numpy (no PyTorch, so it won't match a
  # PyTorch run bit for bit), and reports for each shape how many of 20 seeds
  # reach 100% accuracy and the median accuracy. Needs Python 3.9+ and numpy.
  import itertools

  import numpy as np

  X = np.array(list(itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=8)), float)  # all 256 inputs
  y = X.sum(1) % 2


  def nparams(widths: list[int]) -> int:
      """Parameter count of a dense MLP with these layer widths, biases included."""
      return sum(a * b + b for a, b in zip(widths, widths[1:]))


  def train(
      widths: list[int],
      seed: int,
      steps: int = 4000,
      lr: float = 1e-2,
      wd: float = 1e-4,
  ) -> float:
      """Full-batch AdamW on all 256 inputs; returns the final training accuracy."""
      rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
      P = []    # parameters: W0, b0, W1, b1, ...
      for a, b in zip(widths, widths[1:]):
          bound = 1 / np.sqrt(a)    # same as PyTorch nn.Linear's default init
          P += [rng.uniform(-bound, bound, (a, b)), rng.uniform(-bound, bound, b)]

      m = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]    # Adam first moments
      v = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]    # Adam second moments
      nlayers = len(widths) - 1
      for step in range(1, steps + 1):
          hs = [X]    # hs[i] is the input to layer i
          zs = []     # pre-activations
          h = X
          for i in range(nlayers):
              z = h @ P[2 * i] + P[2 * i + 1]
              zs.append(z)
              h = np.maximum(z, 0) if i < nlayers - 1 else z    # ReLU; linear output
              hs.append(h)

          logit = h[:, 0]
          prob = 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(logit / 2))    # sigmoid without overflow
          g = ((prob - y) / len(y))[:, None]    # d(mean cross-entropy)/d(logit)
          G = [None] * len(P)    # gradients, parallel to P
          for i in reversed(range(nlayers)):
              G[2 * i] = hs[i].T @ g
              G[2 * i + 1] = g.sum(0)
              if i > 0:
                  g = (g @ P[2 * i].T) * (zs[i - 1] > 0)

          # AdamW, using PyTorch's default values for betas (0.9, 0.999) and eps (1e-8)
          for k in range(len(P)):
              P[k] -= lr * wd * P[k]    # decoupled weight decay
              m[k] = 0.9 * m[k] + 0.1 * G[k]
              v[k] = 0.999 * v[k] + 0.001 * G[k] ** 2
              P[k] -= lr * (m[k] / (1 - 0.9 ** step)) / (
                  np.sqrt(v[k] / (1 - 0.999 ** step)) + 1e-8)

      # accuracy of the last forward pass, i.e. before the final update
      return ((logit > 0) == (y > 0.5)).mean()


  for w in [[8, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1], [8, 8, 4, 2, 1], [8, 8, 1], [8, 16, 1], [8, 64, 1]]:
      accs = [train(w, seed) for seed in range(20)]
      print(w, nparams(w), "params; seeds at 100%:", sum(a == 1 for a in accs),
            "/ 20; median acc", np.median(accs))
I might not know enough about ANNs to spot if it's cheating on some way, but it looks legit. It does indeed output that the [8, 64, 1] configuration gets 100% accuracy on all 20 seeds.

↳ reply 2 — krona:

All NN behaviour is emergent strictly speaking; by definition. I think you mean a phase shift of a kind; a qualitative, unpredictable leap in capability.

item.description: 131 points, 47 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (devblogs.microsoft.com)

→ HN comments  ·  131 points  ·  47 comments

Top #1 — olyjohn:

Speaking of getting into Microsoft events, some buddies and I registered with Microsoft as OEM system builders when we were in high school. We would drive to Redmond and attend these events talking about various new hardware and software and would leave with bags full of swag and they had awesome Raffles giving away some expensive shiny new hardware, which we would win quite often shockingly.

We had finally heard about the Microsoft store on campus, and had heard about the super discounted software. Turned out you had to be an employee. We were crushed because retail copies of Win2k were expensive for high schoolers. So we sat out in front of the store with signs "will work for cheap Microsoft software." Finally this girl came by and asked what we were doing, she was an intern or a new hire or something like that not much older than us, still in college. She went into to store and came out with boxed copies of Win2k Workstation for $20 a pop for us. We were stoked and tried to give he some cash, but she was just happy to help us out.

Those were some good times. I wonder if stuff like that still happens today.

↳ reply — kmoser:

My story of getting into a Microsoft event: in late 2000, Microsoft was rebranding MSN with the butterfly logo and they paid groups of inline skaters in NYC to dress up in custom purple velour body suits with wings to skate around Manhattan and generate buzz (heh) about the new MSN.

Well, there happened to be a computer show at the Javits Center so we skated there, convinced a security guard we were with Microsoft (hey, eight skaters in velour MSN body suits must be with Microsoft, right?), and skated onto the show floor. About fifteen minutes later security figured out we weren't part of the show and kicked us out. (We weren't supposed to keep the butterfly outfits but some people did. I didn't keep mine, but I do have photos that prove it really happened.)

then follow the steps already outlined i.e. click on the abstruse Small Business Cybersecurity: Non-Employer Firms (NIST Cybersecurity White Paper 50), which directs to an academic style page with the report.

If anything, the linked page makes it harder to find, since it requires an additional step.

Since this is intended for small business owners with a thousand competing priorities, hiding the guide between walls of text and down a rabbit hole of unfamiliar links and titles will result in significant drop-off.

Top #1 — CobrastanJorji:

> Will it rain over forty percent of the city? Will it rain for forty percent of the day? Or does the speaker just not know and is too shy to say so?

Unrelated, but to answer his question, it's the probability that a random spot in the covered area will get at least a smidge of rain at some point in the covered time period. A 10% chance of rain can mean either that the forecaster is 100% sure that exactly 10% of the area will get rain, or it can mean that the forecaster sees a large rainstorm nearby which would cover the whole area if it arrived, but which only has a 10% chance of arriving. Or anything in between. If there's a rain cloud meandering over the city, covering 1% of the city at a time, and over the whole day it randomly walks over 10% of the city, that's also a 10% chance.

↳ reply — noduerme:

item.description: 127 points, 39 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (polyend.com)

→ HN comments  ·  127 points  ·  39 comments

Top #1 — consumer451:

This has to be related to MWAVE's FM-1 viral popularity, largely due to open firmware right?

https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/from-impulse-purchas...

https://github.com/aroum/fm1-custom-fw

see also:

> Reverse Engineering of the M-VAVE FM-1 Pocket Synthesizer Firmware

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49994065 (75 points - 50 comments)

↳ reply 1 — vvillena:

That, plus the fact people were already poking into the closed firmware binary, plus the existence of an alternative firmware. By doing this, Polyend also kind of passes the responsibility of maintaining the Tracker devices to the community.

It's also worth mentioning that the release is not just a source code release, they added a lot of great features like sample streaming, and dedicated velocity and timing lanes. And they released APIs so that people can easily create new synth engines and effects.

↳↳ reply — mycall:

Bring Roland VSynth capabilities to it.

↳ reply 2 — rickdeckard:

It's more likely because LLM usage and particularly REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) is opening up those firmwares whether the vendor likes it or not.

The best strategy for a HW-vendor at this point is to get ahead of it and open-source the firmware under your own License Agreement, so you can possibly also integrate community work back into your official firmware.

I'm happy that some move in this direction.

The much more terrible strategy is litigation and moving as much logic as possible away from the product into some cloud-service (requiring periodic online-connection, etc.).

We already see both trajectories, so I hope the customers will decide wisely which strategy to fund...

↳ reply 3 — anigbrowl:

Yes. Custom firmware for audio gear has been A Thing for a long time, as far back as the 1990s. I worked on a company that offered a general DSP platform back in 2003, but it didn't take off because it was too difficult for most people to program. JJOS became very popular among users of Akai's MPC line (of whom there are very many) in the mid-2000s.

The combinations of LLMs and agentic reverse-engineering skills have sent things into overdrive in recent months. As well as allowing people to repurpose cheap gear like the M-VAVE it has also revealed that a lot of larger vendors have been outright lying to their users about hardware limitations to more effectively segment their target market. In my the future is high quality controllers/converters with a generic SOC inside. Behringer is already going down this route and has the manufacturing heft to do it quickly and with a decent level of quality. Akai also seems to have jumped in on the trend.

Top #2 — sebastienbarre:

For people afraid of bricking their units, I can't stress enough how groundbreaking it is that they're acknowledging that risk and still offering to repair your unit. You pay of course, because this is a risk you took, but at least they will have a look at it:

    "Out-of-Warranty Repairs Available: In the unlikely event that something ever goes wrong with your hardware while using custom firmware, it is not covered under standard warranty. However, Polyend is always happy to help get your instrument back up and running through its official out-of-warranty repair service (standard service, parts, and shipping fees apply."

↳ reply — mycall:

Does the board come with a jtag interface to unbrick the device?

Top #3 — dimatura:

The avalanche of reverse engineered/custom firmwares is definitely changing the synth landscape. I'm wondering how many other companies will start open sourcing. It isn't always trivial since sometimes there's proprietary software components or toolchains that can't be open sourced. But it's hard to imagine it won't be more common. There's a lot of mixed feelings in the community. A lot of musicians don't like AI, but they do want to have more features and bug fixes. A lot of synth makers are probably ambivalent too, especially if they have a stronger vision of what the synths should be that custom firmware ignore. Not to mention the commercial implications of adding features into existing synths, possibly making newer models less appealing. And of course people are copying UIs and workflows from other synths that took a lot of work to develop.

Yet, anthropic's head count has nearly doubled since last year - so, in a company where nearly half of that head count is engineers, but claude is "writing 90% of the code," what is everyone doing then? Imagine an employee is 1x productive without AI.

Now spend 0.5x their salary on AI, and they become 5x productive compared to no AI.

item.title: US boy names that became girl names and vice versa
item.description: 286 points, 304 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (namedaisy.com)

→ HN comments  ·  286 points  ·  304 comments

Top #1 — ecshafer:

There are a few names I think are being confused. Jan, short for Janice is a female name, but Jan in Central / Eastern Europe as a form of John is masculine. Jean the female name and Jean the french male name are different.

↳ reply 1 — cvhc:

Yeah immigration and mix of similar names from different languages could also be reasons for the (at least perceived) shifts.

↳↳ reply — nostrademons:

This is part of what they mean by girl names driving the shift. You have a traditional ethnic name that may be masculine or feminine and has a baseline low level of popularity. Then you have a popular female name that rapidly gains and loses its popularity. The effect on the mix is that it's shifting from masculine to feminine, but really you should look at it as a newly-popular female name being layered on top of the traditional name. And you can often see this in the timescale, with a clear pop-culture trigger leading to the rising girl name.

Looking at just part of the data, I can see this with Arya (Stark, Game of Thrones), Paris (Hilton), Stevie (Nicks, of Fleetwood Mac), Dakota (Fanning), and Tatum (O'neal), and the masculine trend also relates to the fading of generationally-popular names like Jean (Silent/Boomer), Pat (Boomer), Joan (Silent/Boomer), Courtney (Gen-X/Xennial), etc.

↳ reply 2 — mikepurvis:

I was going to say the same about Jean; I think that one at least is hard to really draw conclusions from without additional data like languages spoken at home.

Anecdotally, the boy->girl names are almost all very popular names where I've met multiple each of those across different ages, whereas the other two categories feel like they have a lot more down-list entries.

↳ reply 3 — dotancohen:

Kim is another good one - I've met several Korean men named Kim.

Though I'm not 100% sure they weren't using their family name as their everyday identity name (the Kims I met were not related).

Top #2 — Fnoord:

My biggest WTF on this (as a foreigner) was the late Lindsey Graham. I always knew Lindsey/Lindsay as a female name.

Either way, peeking through the list, seems to me names which end with a vowel are usually feminine. However, there's a caveat: names end up shortened, and over time even those get shortened.

'Brit', 'Britney' for 'Brittany'.

'Gerry' or 'Geri' or 'Ger' for 'Gareth' (Dutch variant: 'Gerrit'),

'Pat', 'Patty' for 'Patrick', 'Patricia'.

'Pen', 'Penny' for 'Penelope'

'Ash' for 'Ashley'.

'Tash' or 'Tasha' for 'Natasha', 'Nata(s)cha' (a variant of Nathan/Nathaniel?)

'Toni', 'Tony', or 'Ton' for 'Antonia', 'Anton', or 'Antonius'.

Skimming through the quick examples I came up with, one thing stands out: if it ends with an 'a', feminine. I believe this stems from Latin? It also appears Brittany is a very British example, whereas say 'Tony' stems from a Catholic background. People with that background get very traditional names, but they're always practically shortened. Annoyingly, you'd have to mention your complete name on say a form, but otherwise you get a wider choice since you have like three names, and they're relatively long so more variety to pick from.

↳ reply 1 — cestith:

Gerry is also short for Gerald sometimes.

Tony in the US is often short for Anthony.

Chris, Kris, or Cris can be short for Christina, Kristina, Kristofer, Christopher, Kristian, Kristian, Christy, Krista, or Kristi. Sometimes you'll see Crys, Chris, Krys, Kris, or Cris for Crystal/Cristal/Chrystal/Krystal.

You'll also sometimes see Christopher shortened to Topher or to Kit.

↳↳ reply — Fnoord:

Great examples! My initial post is far too limited. It fascinates me, though, like etymology does, too.

'Antony' is also related to 'Antonius' (as is 'Italian Antonio').

One weird one (for me) from English is 'William' -> 'Bill' since there's no 'B' in 'William', and no 'W' in 'Bill'. I wonder what's happening there.

↳↳↳ reply — leipert:

Medieval rhyming stuff. Robert -> Rob. Richard -> Dick. Edward -> Ned.

↳ reply 2 — FranchuFranchu:

Yes, it stems from Latin. See Latin's case declension tables [0]

In Spanish and Portugese, -a is a feminine suffix and -o is masculine; that's where we get Patricio vs Patricia.

There are very few female names that end with -o and very few male names that end with -a in Spanish.

Another example is -ine in Joseph/Josephine. -ine/-ino/-in is a feminizing suffix in German and a diminutive in Spanish and French, that's why it's a femenine suffix in names. In English we have hero vs heroine.

[0]: https://dcc.dickinson.edu/grammar/latin/case-endings-five-de...

Top #3 — petemc_:

There was a guy at my school named Hilary who got awful abuse for it. Always wondered why parents would do such a thing to a child.

↳ reply 1 — ethagnawl:

> And if a man's gonna make it, he's gotta be tough

↳ reply 2 — snarf21:
